Words | Er Mu

Editors | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

When a baby is born, the doctor will try to get it crying, because crying is an important sign that the baby is healthy. Many people think of small children as criers and fussers, sometimes downright annoying, especially in public. But crying really matters to a young child. As the Chinese saying goes, the baby who cries gets the milk. And besides getting itself fed, did you know that crying also helps a child learn to talk sooner? So if you find a crying baby irritating (dads, we’re looking at you), be patient when your little one is crying and fussing, and don’t be too heavy-handed about stopping it. The more they cry, the sooner you may hear them call out “mama” or “dada.” Of course, this article isn’t really here to lecture dads; it’s here to talk about how babies and toddlers develop the ability to listen and speak.

Speech involves two abilities, listening and speaking, and to learn to speak, a child first has to hear and understand what others are saying. Hearing is also the first of the two that a baby has. In fact, in terms of organ development, a newborn’s speech organs are less mature than its auditory system. The whole vocal apparatus, larynx and throat included, is still immature; the shape and position of the vocal tract are very different from an adult’s, and the larynx sits high, closer to where it is in a gorilla.

Did somebody mention me?

The higher the larynx, the harder the tongue is to control, and the harder it is to articulate. So even when a child is mentally ready to talk, its still-developing speech organs won’t let it speak clearly. From about the third month, the larynx gradually descends, and it doesn’t reach full maturity until around the age of four.

Positions of the vocal organs in a gorilla and an adult human

Listening

On the latest season of Roast!, a Chinese celebrity roast show, one comedian took aim at the hottest after-school activity of the moment: coding classes for kids. It brings to mind the earlier craze for all sorts of prenatal education classes. (Parents everywhere mean well, and nobody wants their child to fall behind at the starting line. Beijing school-district apartments, anyone?) One of these is prenatal music education. So how early can a fetus hear sound? And does playing it music actually do anything?

Generally speaking, a fetus starts to perceive sound at around 24 weeks, and a few weeks later it can hear sounds within a bandwidth of one octave. An adult’s audible range spans ten octaves, so this is about a tenth of an adult’s bandwidth.

Most of the sounds a fetus first hears in the womb have to do with its mother: her voice, her heartbeat and the sounds of her digestive system, all mixed together. These sounds have to travel through the amniotic fluid to reach the fetus’s ears, so they come through muffled, like hearing people talk on the shore while you are underwater. Studies have shown that playing these “womb sounds” to premature babies in neonatal intensive care does lower their heart rate and help them settle. Another study found that playing the mother’s voice, muffled in the same way, inside the incubator helps the auditory cortex of premature babies to develop.

So womb sounds do benefit premature babies. What about fetuses developing normally? As in the picture further up, a pair of headphones is placed on the mother’s belly and a selection of music is played. To date, there is no clear evidence that this helps fetal development [1]. On the contrary, we may need to worry whether this extra sound could damage the hearing of a fetus developing normally in the womb, because we still don’t know how loud a sound it can tolerate. So does prenatal music education work? Is it good or bad for fetal development? There really is no scientific answer yet, and until there is, perhaps the most natural approach is the best.

Speaking

All babbling starts with crying. One study of 9,000 newborns found that in the first few weeks, a newborn cries for about two hours a day on average, falling to about an hour a day by the twelfth week. This crying matters for developing speech: it is the most basic vocal practice, and every cry contains rises and falls in pitch and loudness.

A newborn’s cries: sound pressure over time (top) and spectrogram (bottom)

The upper half of the figure shows how the sound pressure of a newborn’s cries varies over time, and the lower half is the corresponding spectrogram. Look closely and you can see many parallel dark lines: these are the harmonics of the cry, and their rise and fall is the rise and fall in pitch we hear when a baby cries. As mentioned at the start, a newborn’s vocal organs are not yet fully developed, and it cannot yet control its vocal folds well; all it can do is control how hard air is pushed out of the lungs, that is, how hard it breathes. At this stage, the movement of the vocal folds is governed entirely by the Bernoulli effect (the faster the flow, the lower the pressure). When air from the lungs passes through the narrow glottis, it speeds up, and by Bernoulli’s principle the pressure at the vocal folds drops, pulling them shut; but the air pushing up from behind forces them open again. This cycle repeats over and over, setting the vocal folds in motion and producing sound. The harder the baby breathes, the faster the vocal folds open and close, and the higher and louder the sound.

Although babies’ nervous systems are not yet developed enough to control the vocal folds well, varying how hard they breathe already makes their voices malleable. In fact, from birth, every baby’s cry really is different, with its own personality and character. Where do these traits come from? Research shows they are closely linked to the “womb sounds” the baby heard while still inside its mother.

A German research team compared the cries of newborns in Germany and in France and found that French newborns’ cries reach their highest pitch a little later than German newborns’ cries do. The different melodic contours of the two kinds of cry closely mirror the two languages. In French, a sentence usually rises in pitch all the way to the end before falling;

# Je suis bien contente que ça vous plaise.

# I’m so glad you like it.

whereas in German, the pitch falls at many points within a single sentence.

# Gib jedem Tag die Chance, der schönste deines Lebens zu werden!

# Give every day the chance to become the most beautiful day of your life!

Five languages compared: “passionate” German

In other words, while still in the womb, these newborns were already perceiving and learning the intonation of their mothers’ speech.

The pitch of a baby’s cry generally lies between 250 and 450 Hz, but sometimes babies produce louder, higher sounds that reach 1,000–2,000 Hz. Besides these two kinds of continuous sound, a baby’s cry also contains intermittent creaky sounds (creaky quality), visible in the second half of the spectrogram above. In the first few months, a baby’s cries are all combinations of these three kinds of sound. Later, as the vocal organs and nervous system mature, babies gain better and better control of the muscles they use to vocalize, and their cries can carry richer information, such as discomfort or hunger.

A baby’s crying is usually seen as a negative signal: something is bothering them. But one day the baby may suddenly cry especially hard, in long bouts, and if you listen carefully you can hear that each cry is made up of several shorter segments, with a certain melody to it. This kind of intonation is an important feature of language. When a baby can break up a cry by briefly closing the glottis, it means they can already chunk sound into segments, and this ability to chunk means that before long they will say their first word, which, more often than not, is “MAMA.”

References

1 Caveat emptor; this paper involves a manufacturer of a product. López-Teijón, M., García-Faura, Á. and Prats-Galino, A., 2015. ‘Fetal facial expression in response to intravaginal music emission’. Ultra sound, 23(4), pp. 216–23.

2 Cox, Trevor. Now You're Talking. Random House.
